title: SSL pinning in a mobile app
tagline: Pin the server's key, so a proxy holding a trusted certificate still reads nothing.
intro: TLS proves the certificate is signed by a trusted CA. Pinning adds a second question: is it the key we expect?

sections.title: What it does
sections.summary: One extra check, after the normal one passes.

blocks.caption: The pin check runs after the chain is already valid.

items.label: Mismatch → abort

items: Stops a proxy whose CA was installed on the device — Charles, mitmproxy, an MDM profile.
Stops a compromised or mis-issuing CA signing a certificate for your domain.
Does not stop a rooted device: Frida can patch the check out.
Raises the cost of intercepting traffic. It is not a wall.

sections.summary: What a coffee-shop network can do to an app that trusts the device.

items: The session token in the Authorization header, replayable from anywhere.
Every request body: credentials at login, personal data after it.
The responses too — a balance, a price or a feature flag rewritten before the app sees it.
Nothing looks wrong to the user: the padlock is there and the certificate is valid.

body: The device is not compromised and the user did nothing careless. Trusting one extra CA is enough, and a captive portal is a normal-looking place to be asked.

sections.title: What to pin
sections.summary: Three choices, and only one of them survives renewal.

rows: Every renewal, so a few times a year.
Only when the key pair itself changes.
The CA rotates its intermediate, without telling you.
Weak: anyone with a cert from that CA passes.

blocks.caption: Read the SPKI pin off the live server

sections.title: How the app compares the key
sections.summary: Where the pin comes from, and what is actually compared.

blocks.caption: Two sources, reduced the same way, compared as strings.

items.label: Build time
items.detail: You read the key off the server you control

items.label: Runtime
items.detail: The certificate the peer just sent

items.label: SPKI → SHA-256 → base64
items.detail: The same reduction on both sides

items.label: Equal
items.detail: The peer holds the key you pinned

items.label: Different
items.detail: Connection aborted

items: Take the certificate the server presented, in DER form.
Cut out the SubjectPublicKeyInfo: the public key plus its algorithm id, not the whole certificate.
SHA-256 over exactly those bytes.
Base64 the digest — that is the sha256/… string in your pin list.
Compare against the pins compiled into the app. Any match passes; no match drops the connection.
The app never discovers the key — you put it there, read once from the server you control.
That is the whole trust anchor: the pin is believed because it shipped with the app, not because the network said so.
TLS does the other half: the server must sign the handshake with the matching private key, so presenting a certificate is not enough.
A copy of your certificate is therefore useless to an attacker. The private key never leaves the server.
Most libraries test every certificate in the chain, so a pin may name the leaf key or its issuer.

body: Hashing the whole certificate instead of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo is the classic mistake: the digest then changes at every renewal, even when the key did not.

sections.title: Always ship a backup pin
sections.summary: This is the section that decides whether pinning ever bricks your app.

blocks.caption: The app already trusts the next key before the server switches to it.

items.label: Pin A
items.detail: Key in use today

items.label: Pin B
items.detail: Next key, generated early, kept offline

items.label: Both ship in the release
items.detail: The app accepts either

items.label: Server moves to key B
items.detail: Installed apps keep working

items.label: Next release adds pin C
items.detail: And the cycle repeats

items: A single pin means the day the key changes, every installed app stops working.
Users on old versions cannot be fixed by a server change — only by a store update.
Generate the backup key now and keep it offline; a pin for a key you own is useless if it is lost with the server.
Pin only your own API. Third-party SDKs rotate on their schedule, not yours.

sections.title: Android
sections.summary: Config for the whole app, or OkHttp for one client.

blocks.caption: res/xml/network_security_config.xml — expiration disables the pin instead of killing the app

body: Point android:networkSecurityConfig at the file in the manifest, or nothing is enforced.

items: By hand it is a URLSessionDelegate that hashes the SPKI of the leaf and compares.
Never call completionHandler(.useCredential, …) without comparing — that turns pinning off.
TrustKit also reports failures, which is how you find a bad rollout early.

body: badCertificateCallback is not pinning. It only runs after validation already failed, and returning true there weakens TLS instead of strengthening it.

blocks.caption: Trust only your own CA, nothing the device trusts

items: This pins the CA, so renewing the leaf under the same CA keeps working.
For SPKI pinning use a package that hashes the key, and ship two hashes.
Bundle the .pem as an asset; do not fetch it over the network you are protecting.

sections.title: Prove it works
sections.summary: A pin you never tested is a pin you do not have.

items: Run mitmproxy and install its CA on the device or simulator.
Open the app without pinning: requests appear in the proxy.
Turn pinning on and repeat: the calls must fail, not merely look empty.
Change one pin to a wrong value and confirm the app fails closed.
Test on a release build. Debug builds often trust user CAs and hide the result.
Add a test that fails if the pin list is empty, so a bad merge cannot silently disable it.

rows: The key changes and every installed app is dead until users update.
Anyone who buys a certificate from that CA passes the check.
Analytics or payments break on their rotation schedule, not yours.
No expiry and no kill switch
A bad pin can only be fixed by a store release, which takes days.
